1:
Henry raises the question the whole chapter poses and leaves it open. Whether these rules for public worship were designed to be observed even where they differ from the law of Moses, and whether they were so observed under the second temple, he says is not certain; and he notes that the history of the later Jewish church does not show them governing their worship by these ordinances, as one would have expected, but only by the law of Moses, treating this vision in the next age as mystical rather than literal. Keil and Delitzsch treat the passage structurally instead, as directions for the prince's conduct at the offering of sacrifices which it had already devolved on him to provide. Clarke gives the plan of the chapter in a line, the ordinances of worship for prince and people, the gifts the prince may bestow, and the courts for boiling the holy oblations.

The gate and its opening are described with care. Ellicott notes that the outer gate on the east had already been ordered shut except for the prince, and that the same is now commanded for the east gate of the inner court, with the days specified on which the prince shall use it. Henry adds the contrast that gives the rule its point, that while the other gates of the court were opened every day this one was opened only on high days and on special occasions. Gill supplies the mystical reading Henry had mentioned as belonging to a later age, taking the eastern gate of the priests' court, to design the ministry of the Gospel, which is a ministry of reconciliation holding forth Christ.

Ellicott traces the prince's movements exactly and marks the limit set to them. He enters the sanctuary by the east gate of the outer court, crosses that court to the inner gate, and worships at the threshold immediately adjoining the inner court while the priests make ready his sacrifices; but he is not to enter the inner court himself or to assume any priestly function. Of the people Ellicott is equally exact: so far as they are present on the sabbaths and new moons they are not to worship in the same place as the prince but in the outer court, at the entrance of the east gate to the inner one. Gill reads their worship devotionally rather than topographically, as attending the ministration of word and ordinances with constancy and fervency,. Wesley glosses the sabbaths as taking in both the weekly day and the other holy days called by that name.

All three who count the animals notice that the numbers do not agree with the law, and Ellicott alone notices that they diverge in opposite directions. The sabbath burnt offering under the law was two lambs, and here it is greatly increased, the meat offering for the ram being enlarged too while that for the lambs is left to the prince's generosity; but for the new moon the law required two bullocks, seven lambs and a ram, so that what is appointed here is diminished, and the he-goat for a sin offering that the law required is not mentioned at all. Gill makes the same observation about the single bullock of the new moon, and Clarke states generally that this proportion of offerings differs from the Mosaic prescription, glossing the clause about the prince's hand as meaning according to his ability, to what the providence of God has put within his power. Clarke draws a political lesson from the prince's obligation as well: the chief magistrate was bound to attend the public worship of God as much as the priest, to show that the civil and ecclesiastical states are under one government, and that no man is capable of being either prince or priest who does not acknowledge God in all his ways.
9:
The rule about entering by one gate and leaving by the opposite is explained the same way by three of them. Ellicott says the first provision is for securing order in a vast concourse, since at the solemn feasts all the males of Israel were commanded to be present and the numbers were therefore very large. Wesley offers the same reason more tentatively, that it was perhaps only to prevent jostling and confusion. Clarke works out the geometry: the north and south gates being opposite each other, whoever entered by the one had to leave by the other, no one was to come in at the east gate since there was no gate at the west, and nobody was permitted to turn round and go out where he had come in. Keil and Delitzsch state the rule plainly without comment.

What it means that the prince is in the midst of them is read three ways. Ellicott makes it a change of function: at these yearly feasts it was no longer necessary for the prince to represent the people, since they were present themselves, so he now worships among them, entering with them by the north or south gate and going out by the opposite one. Clarke keeps the emphasis on the discipline rather than the representation, that the prince must go straight forward like everyone else and never turn back to leave by the gate he entered, and that prince and people were to begin and end their worship at the same time. Gill takes the phrase typologically and gathers a series of parallels: the prince in the midst of a worshipping people answers to the descriptions of Christ as the Angel in the midst of the burning bush, as standing among the myrtle trees, as walking among the golden candlesticks, and as the tree of life in the midst of the paradise of God.

Ellicott then notes what the following verses are for. The proportions of the meat offering already laid down are repeated here for the feast days, with the addition that the same is to hold for all established seasons, a different proportion being prescribed only for the daily sacrifice. He also points out a case still unprovided for, that the prince might offer a voluntary burnt offering or peace offering at any time as any of the people might; in that case he still enters by the east gate, but the gate, instead of standing open until evening as on the sabbaths and new moons, is to be shut immediately after. Gill reads the same voluntary offering as belonging to week days as distinguished from sabbaths and new moons and solemnities, and applies it to weekday lectures as distinct from the weekly and monthly stated times of ministry.

On the daily offering, two of them notice the same divergence from the older law and notice that it runs in both directions at once. Clarke states the omission bluntly, that the evening offering is left out entirely, which makes an important difference between this and the old ordinances. Ellicott gives the whole comparison: the victim is the same as under the law, but where that required it morning and evening this provides only for the morning, while on the other hand the accompanying meat offering is increased from a tenth of an ephah of flour to a sixth. Keil and Delitzsch render the same regulations and mark the closing words as everlasting statutes perpetually enduring. Gill takes the shift to the plural at the end as decisive for the reference of the whole passage: it shows that not a single person is meant in the preceding verses but all the Lord's people, who are all priests to God and are to offer up spiritual sacrifices daily.
16:
The rule about the prince's gifts is explained by its purpose, and the purposes offered differ. Ellicott treats the whole as a provision against the alienation of the royal domain: the prince was to have a portion of land on either side of the sacred oblation, ample enough to prevent any attempt on his part at violence and exaction, and for that same reason the territory had to remain inalienably in his family. Henry reads it as a law limiting the prince's power over the crown lands, allowing a deserving son some part settled on him and his heirs provided it does not pass out of the family. Keil and Delitzsch state the distinction that governs both readings, that a gift to a son is inheritance and remains with his sons, while a gift to a servant belongs to him only until the year of liberty and then reverts to the prince. Clarke identifies that year as the jubilee, so called because there was then a general release, servants receiving liberty and alienated estates returning to their owners; Wesley says the same, that whatever lands are given to servants revert at the jubilee to the prince's sons and to theirs after them.

Gill takes the two classes of recipient typologically. The servants who are not sons he makes the unregenerate ministers who preach Christ in pretence rather than in reality, together with carnal professors who have only the outside of religion; and on the warning against oppression he turns the sentence into a promise, that Christ the Prince will never take any part of his people's inheritance from them nor thrust them out of the possession of any blessing of grace. Ellicott keeps the warning as a warning, a fresh caution against oppression and a reminder that the territory given inalienably to the prince exists to provide his sons' inheritance.

The closing description of the kitchens is set out most fully by Ellicott, who explains why two sets of them were needed. The people could partake only of the peace offerings, whereas the priests, besides their portion of these, were required to consume the flesh of the sin and trespass offerings and the greater part of the meat offerings; hence one place near the priests' chambers and others in the corners of the outer court. He adds a nicety about the prohibition against carrying the holy things out, that although the priestly chambers and these cooking rooms stood within the area of the outer court they were reckoned, with the walk leading to them, as belonging to the inner. Henry supplies the plain reason for the whole arrangement, that one who kept so plentiful a table at his altar needed large kitchens, and that a wise builder provides conveniences of that kind.

Two details are contested. Gill reports that the word rendered joined is understood by others as made with chimneys, so that the smoke of the kitchen fires and the steam of the boiling flesh might have a way to ascend, which he notes is the general rabbinic reading. Ellicott describes the arrangement differently, as tables of masonry fixed around the walls of these enclosures with boiling places underneath, and Wesley as a range of building on the inside of the walls of the lesser courts. Clarke ends with what the places were used for and what came of it: they were uncovered apartments where fires were kept for dressing those portions of the peace offerings which individuals brought through a principle of devotion, on which their families and friends afterwards feasted, while portions were sent to the poor and the widows and the fatherless — so that the spirit of devotion became the means of preserving the spirit of mercy.
